items.title: What It Would Actually Take for a Machine to Have Agency (Michael Tomasello)
items.creator: Machine Learning Street Talk
items.topic: agency in animals, children and machines
items.description: Developmental psychologist Michael Tomasello, who spent twenty years comparing children and great apes, explains when nature builds a decision maker instead of a fixed reflex, and what that means for machines.
items.why_recommended: Agents are everywhere in AI right now. This is a rare outside view from someone who studied real agency for decades.
items.connection_to_interests: AI agents, planning and cognitive science.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: A clear test for agency: unpredictability calls for a decision maker. Use it on any system that claims to be an agent.

cross_domain.connection: Tomasello traces agency from control loops in reptiles to a squirrel imagining a fall to apes seeking more information. Each step is a design question for AI agents: when should a system stop and decide?

items.title: We've been asking: "What if AI solved the Riemann Hypothesis?"
items.creator: 3Blue1Brown
items.topic: mathematicians react to AI and the Riemann Hypothesis
items.description: Short takes from mathematicians including Kevin Buzzard, Terence Tao, Daniel Litt and Jordan Ellenberg on a recent announcement tied to the Riemann Hypothesis and what AI means for mathematics.
items.why_recommended: The strongest video of the week by engagement, and a fast way to hear careful experts rather than headlines. Note the on-screen correction at 13:20.
items.connection_to_interests: AI for science, mathematical reasoning and evaluation.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: How working mathematicians judge a claimed breakthrough, and what checking an AI-assisted proof actually takes.

items.title: After Life (1998)
items.creator: Hirokazu Kore-eda
items.topic: choosing one memory to keep forever
items.description: In a quiet way station, the newly dead have one week to choose a single memory, which staff then recreate on film. Kore-eda mixes actors with real people telling their own memories.
items.why_recommended: A gentle, deeply human Japanese film. Chosen for its emotional depth, not its fame.
items.connection_to_interests: Japanese cinema, memory and understanding people.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: A quiet evening, and a question to carry: which single memory would you keep, and why that one?

cross_domain.connection: The film turns a question about memory into a production process. People revise, embellish and rebuild their memories on set, which is close to what memory research says we do every time we remember.

items.title: Neural Networks, Manifolds, and Topology
items.creator: Chris Olah
items.topic: what layers do to the shape of data
items.description: A visual essay on neural network layers as transformations that stretch and fold data, and on what topology says a network of a given width can and cannot separate.
items.why_recommended: Pairs with today's horned sphere video. An older essay that still shapes how interpretability researchers think. This link is an archived copy.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: A geometric picture of what a classifier does to its input, and why some datasets need extra dimensions to untangle.

cross_domain.connection: Topology asks which shapes can be deformed into each other. Olah uses that question to explain why a network sometimes cannot separate two classes, linking abstract maths to representation learning.

items.title: Chichu Art Museum, Naoshima
items.creator: Tadao Ando (architect), Benesse Art Site
items.topic: a museum built almost entirely underground
items.description: A museum on a small island in Japan's Seto Inland Sea, set mostly underground and lit by daylight. It holds a few works by Monet, James Turrell and Walter De Maria.
items.duration: half a day if you go, 20 min to explore online
items.why_recommended: One of the clearest examples of a building designed around light and attention. Worth a slow look at photos even if a trip is far off.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: A feel for how architecture can slow you down, and an idea for a future trip in Japan.

items.title: Carlo Rovelli on the Nature of Reality
items.creator: Philosophy Bites
items.topic: is there an ultimate reality science converges on
items.description: Physicist and philosopher Carlo Rovelli talks with Nigel Warburton about whether science is slowly getting closer to one ultimate picture of reality.
items.why_recommended: Short, dense and new this week. A good walk-length episode on a question every scientist quietly assumes an answer to.
items.connection_to_interests: Philosophy of science and modern physics.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: A sharper sense of what it means for a theory to be true, and a relational way of thinking about reality you can bring to debates.

items.title: In Our Time: Epic of Gilgamesh
items.creator: BBC Radio 4, Melvyn Bragg
items.topic: the oldest surviving great work of literature
items.description: Melvyn Bragg and guests on Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, and Enkidu: a story kept on cuneiform tablets for thousands of years, then lost, then pieced back together after 1853.
items.why_recommended: An archive episode re-released this week. Pairs well with the Ishtar episode from the same show if you want more.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: The story of Gilgamesh in outline, and how scholars rebuilt a lost epic from broken clay tablets.

items.title: Japan's (linguistic) KATSU obsession EXPLAINED!
items.creator: Japan Station
items.topic: everyday Japanese words ending in katsu
items.description: An English-language episode on why so many Japanese words end in katsu, activity: club life, job hunting, marriage hunting, therapeutic crying and even a corn boom.
items.why_recommended: Explained in English, so it suits a beginner. One word ending opens a window on daily life in Japan.
items.connection_to_interests: Japanese culture and everyday life, linguistics.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: A handful of real words people use every day, and a feel for how Japanese builds new words from one kanji.

items.title: MIT 6.S184: Flow Matching and Diffusion Models, Lecture 01: Flow and Diffusion Models (2026)
items.creator: Peter Holderrieth and Ron Shprints, MIT
items.topic: flow matching and diffusion from first principles
items.description: First lecture of MIT's course on generative AI with differential equations. It builds flow and diffusion models from the maths up, with lecture notes, slides and code exercises.
items.why_recommended: Very high views for the channel's size, and it goes beyond intuition to the actual framework. Free notes and exercises let you go deeper.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: A unified picture of diffusion and flow models as learned vector fields, solid enough to read new papers in this area.

items.title: This Object Defies Common Sense
items.creator: Numberphile, with Richard Elwes
items.description: Mathematician Richard Elwes explains the Alexander horned sphere, a strange surface that shows how intuition about inside and outside can fail in three dimensions.
items.why_recommended: A gentle, visual step into topology, with a high comment rate for the channel.
items.connection_to_interests: Topology, one of your growth subjects.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: A famous counterexample you can picture, and why topologists care so much about well-behaved spaces.

items.title: Old trams waste power on purpose. Here's why
items.creator: Tom Scott
items.topic: how old trams are driven, plus a tram driving contest
items.description: Tom Scott explains why old trams burn off power by design, then holds his own tram driving championship with the Seaton Tramway team.
items.why_recommended: Pure free-time fun with a real engineering idea inside. Strong likes for its size.
items.connection_to_interests: Strange science, history of technology and unexpected connections.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: A small, memorable piece of engineering history, and half an hour of good-natured competition.

items.title: You and Your Research
items.creator: Richard Hamming
items.topic: how great research careers are made
items.description: Transcript of Hamming's 1986 talk at Bellcore on why some scientists do great work: picking important problems, open doors, courage and turning obstacles into assets.
items.why_recommended: A classic worth reading once a year. On a day full of AI and maths, it asks the question behind them all: what is worth working on?
items.connection_to_interests: Research taste and generating research ideas.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: A personal list of the important problems in your field, and one habit to try this week.

items.title: Entangled Life: How Fungi Make Our Worlds, Change Our Minds and Shape Our Futures
items.creator: Merlin Sheldrake
items.description: A biologist's book on fungi: the networks linking plant roots, lichens as partnerships between species, and how fungi blur the line between individual and community.
items.why_recommended: Genuinely unfamiliar territory, written with wonder. Read one chapter, the lichen chapter is a good place to start.
items.connection_to_interests: Evolutionary biology, nature observation and strange science.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: A new view of what counts as an organism, and why lichens made biologists rethink the idea of a single individual.

items.title: Talking Timbuktu
items.creator: Ali Farka Touré with Ry Cooder
items.topic: Malian desert blues meets American slide guitar
items.description: A 1994 album recorded by Malian guitarist Ali Farka Touré and Ry Cooder in a few days. Slow, hypnotic songs that show how close West African music and the blues are.
items.why_recommended: Beautiful background for work or a walk, from a region you rarely hear from. It won a Grammy for world music.
items.connection_to_interests: Music appreciation and cultures beyond your usual map.
items.what_i_might_get_from_it: An hour of calm music, and an ear for how the blues may echo older West African traditions.
